page_title: No code reviews by default - Raycast Blog

summary.title: No code reviews by default - Raycast Blog
summary.one_liner: Raycast's engineers push straight to the main branch and request code reviews only when needed, a trust-based workflow supported by continuous integration and nightly internal releases.
takeaways: Raycast does not require code reviews; engineers push to the main branch and request reviews only when they think it is necessary.
The team argues pull requests discourage trust, do not reliably catch bugs, and slow work down.
Nightly internal releases, continuous integration on every commit, and feature flags let the team dogfood changes within about 24 hours.
Reviews are still requested for risky areas such as first-time database migrations and for new team members during their first few weeks.
A post-commit message in Slack or on GitHub can notify teammates of changes without blocking on a review; the author notes this may not suit teams with strict security requirements.
summary.summary: The post describes how Raycast moved from informal trust-based work between its two founders to a fully distributed team that skips mandatory pull requests. It lays out the reasons the team rejected PRs (less trust, no reliable bug prevention, slower progress) and the workflow that replaces them: direct pushes to main, every commit built and tested by CI, a nightly internal release installed for the whole team, and feature flags to keep unfinished work internal. The author also covers exceptions, such as reviews for new parts of the codebase, and advises readers to question best practices rather than adopt them dogmatically.
